podcasts.name: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Inventor of Liturgical Chanting
podcast.body: Hildegard von Bingen basically invented the sound of standard liturgical chanting heard in Catholic churches, cathedrals, and monasteries starting around the 12th century. Her style, known officially as sacred monophony, was characterized by slow, somber melodies perfectly suited to the long reverberation times of large gothic cathedrals, influencing composers for centuries on how to use architectural acoustics to enhance music. "Hilogart basically invented the sound of standard liturgical chanting that began to be heard in Catholic churches, cathedrals, and monasteries, starting in about the 12th century."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Mother of Science in Germany
podcast.body: Hildegard von Bingen, born in 1098 in what is now modern Germany, was a nun, mystic, and visionary, with some considering her to be the "mother of science" in Germany. Her wide-ranging influence extended beyond music to various intellectual fields. "Some even consider her to be the mother of science in Germany, but she was also a composer of a special type of sacred music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Roots of Modern Gothic Music (1987)
xref.body: The Sisters of Mercy, specifically with a song from 1987, are used to illustrate the historical lineage of modern gothic music. The roots of this compositional style are traced back over 800 years to Hildegard von Bingen's sacred monophony, composed around 1156, and its suitability for performance in massive stone cathedrals. "Yes, that's the systems of mercy from 1987, but the roots of that kind of composition go back to 1156."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
